1394.prule: Lexical tone language (H, L, HL, LH etc. lexical melodies / per-syllable tones; Leben 1973 vs Dwyer 1978 debate is about the representation of tone, both treat Mende as tonal). No word-stress rule in the modern analysis. The only 'accent' statement is Migeod 1908 (pre-tonal): penultimate accent, shifting to the final syllable in the definite singular (-i suffix).
1394.srule: Not mentioned in Dwyer 1978 (SAL 9(2):167-208, secs. 1-7 read in full): a tone-only analysis with no secondary or rhythmic stress; the word 'stress' occurs only in a rejected hypothetical tone-mapping rule for English loans (pp.178-179). Migeod 1908:48 (historical) gives one penultimate accent per word and no secondary accent.

For Mende the tonal "melody" is stored in the "suprasegmental" component and the remaining phonological information in the segmental component. ... Leben has repeatedly claimed for example that Mende is such a language requiring a melodic analysis ... In this paper, the predictions of the "melodic" proposal are compared against an alternative proposal which claims that the tones of Mende are never completely…

1394.idn: Dwyer: 'Mende' (no narrower variety; he notes Innes's transcriptions 'apparently represent a slightly different dialect' from 'the dialect described by Spears', p.176); Migeod: 'the southern form of speech' of Mende, Sierra Leone Protectorate (Kpa Mende on the west and Pokpa on the east named but not studied)…
1394.exq_: (No stress rule in the tonal analysis. Migeod 1908:48 on his accent rule: 'The very few exceptions are specially marked in this book.')
1394.tone: Mende is the textbook autosegmental tone language (Leben 1973 five melodies H, L, HL, LH, LHL; Dwyer 1978 argues for per-syllable tones, max two per syllable, and reconstructs Proto-SW-Mande as a 'partially free pitch-accent system' historically). Dwyer mentions 'penultimate stress' only as a rejected hypothetical mapping rule for English loans (p.178, sec. 3.4.3; examples (8a-b) on p.179: 'high tones are assigned from left to right up to and including the penultimate syllable and a low tone is assigned to the ultimate... clear counterexamples also exist'). Migeod 1908 (pre-tonal, no mention of tone at all) heard a penultimate 'accent' moving to the final syllable in the definite singular; this is best read as an impression of the tonal/definite-suffix pattern, not an independent stress system.

1396.heavy: 'heavier than the penultimate, i.e. the final syllable has more segments than the previous syllable' — a relative segment-count criterion; exemplified by a final diphthong (la»rai, CVV) and a final closed syllable (ma»lim, CVC) outweighing a CV penult. 1396.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable, but on the final syllable when the final syllable is heavier than the penult (heavier = has more segments than the preceding syllable, e.g. final diphthong la»rai or final closed syllable ma»lim vs. CV penult). Stress not contrastive.

1397.dq: Accent placement is restricted to the first or second syllable of a phonological word.
1397.prule: Culminative pitch-accent (high pitch, fall after the accented syllable), one per phonological word, restricted to the first or second syllable; placement within that two-syllable window is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs tábo 'snake' vs tabó 'neck', kíkem vs kikém, etc.); majority of words accent the second syllable.
1397.srule: Possible secondary accent, not analysed: after the high-pitch primary accent (syllable 1 or 2) the syllable on which pitch falls from mid to low 'could be signalling what is sometimes referred to as secondary stress... Further research is required in this area'; no placement rule given, except that it does not correspond to a morphological boundary (bodomolam vs bakyamu-da).

There are a number of minimal pairs which contrast solely through accent placement. What exactly is meant by 'accent'? There is no consensus amongst linguists who have worked on the language as to what feature or bundle of features mark the 'accent'. Bartos (1977) refers to the feature …

1398.prule: Stress is root-bound: each root carries an inherent stressed syllable (the root syllable proper; the stem-formative/thematic suffix syllable is 'átona'); in compounds primary stress falls on the first root, the second root loses its stress (or keeps a secondary stress on its first syllable). Three lexical tones (high, low, rising) contrast only on the first syllable of the root; suffix syllables have no tonal opposition.
1398.srule: Only in compounds: in compounds of two disyllabic roots the second root keeps a secondary stress on its first syllable ('Hay un acento secundario en la primera sílaba de la segunda raíz', 14.2); in compounds of two monosyllabic roots the second root loses its stress (14.1). No rhythmic secondary stress is described for simplex words; the 'acento en la última sílaba de una frase' is a phrase-level accent (see domain note).

1399.prule: quantity-insensitive, syllable-count rule: iterative iambs right-to-left with rightmost foot extrametrical and main stress only on a branching foot. Primary stress word-final in words of 1-3 syllables; antepenultimate in words of 4+ syllables. Secondary stress on the initial syllable of trisyllables; in 4+ syllable words secondary stresses alternate in both directions from the primary, with the final syllable always (secondarily) stressed (attributed to final lengthening).
1399.srule: Secondary stress on the first syllable of 3-syllable words; in words of 4+ syllables secondary stresses on alternating syllables in both directions from the antepenultimate primary, so the final syllable always bears secondary stress (and the initial syllable in odd-parity words); heads of iterative R-to-L iambs, the extrametrical final foot's head heard as stressed through final lengthening.

1400.dq: in all uncompounded words the chief accent fell upon the stem-syllable and always remained there even when suffixes and inflexional endings followed it.
1400.dloc: sec. 25 'Stress (Accent)', p. 15; prefixes (noun/adj. vs. verb accent): sec. 156, pp. 78-79; secondary accent on suffixes: sec. 138, pp. 69-70; French loans: sec. 186 (p. 95), sec. 215 (p. 103), cross-ref sec. 230 (p. 105)
1400.prule: Native words: chief accent on the stem (root) syllable, immovable under suffixation and inflection (Germanic root-syllable stress); compounds: stem syllable of the first member when the second member is a noun/adjective, stem syllable of the second member when it is a verb or deverbal. French (AN./O.Fr.) loans: the Romance tonic accent was shifted back onto an earlier (pretonic) syllable in ME, the old tonic syllable keeping a secondary accent for a time.
1400.srule: Secondary accent (Wright 1928): in native words on heavy suffixal/derivative syllables (-dom, -er(e), -fast, -fold (-fald), -ful, -hede, -ing, -isch, -les, -liche, -ling, -lok, -schipe, -sum, -ung, -ward: kinedom, wisdom, stedefast, frendschipe) and on second elements of compounds (alderman, chapman); in trisyllables on the second or third syllable by formation (laffdi, frendschip(e) vs. Fridai, kinedom); gradually lost during ME. In early French loans the originally tonic syllable kept a secondary accent for a time after the accent shift, later lost. Placement morphological, not rhythmic. (Modern restatement: Germanic feet built left to right give secondary-stressed feet in longer words, none on final syllables -- Fikkert, Dresher & Lahiri 2006 sec. 5.)

evidence_works.detail: Chronology of English stress in which Middle English keeps the Germanic setting: '(14) Approximate dates of changes in direction and position of English stress a. Gmc.–Middle Eng.: Foot direction left, main stress left; b. c1570: Foot direction is changing to right. c. c1660–: Main stress changes to right in stages.' (ms. p.10, (14)). On the French loans: 'It can be shown that the influx of Anglo-Norman and Old French words following the Norman conquest made little impact on Middle English prosody (Minkova 1997; Redford 2003; Dresher & Lahiri 2005; Lahiri 2015), contrary to what has sometimes been claimed.' (ms. p.11). The paper's own new evidence is on Early Modern English (Levins 1570 and the count of stress-affecting Latinate suffixes); its Middle English statement is a summary that cites the four works named, so it is entered as cites-for-stress. Adds to the entry: the dated end-point of the left-edge system (foot direction changing c1570, main stress c1660 on), and the explicit claim that the French loans did not change ME prosody, which agrees with the entry's Wright & Wright sec. 186 / sec. 215 statement that the borrowed words shifted their accent.

evidence_works.work: Dresher & Lahiri 2005, Main Stress Left in Early Middle English (Historical Linguistics 2003, CILT 257: 75-85)
evidence_works.detail: Metrical (foot-based) analysis of Old and Middle English stress on philological material (OE/ME word forms, Chaucer's verse stressings, dated Romance loans and their Present Day English reflexes). Germanic setting: '(1) Germanic: Stress on the stem-initial syllable, regardless of quantity, building secondary stress from left to right.' (ms. p.2). Foot: 'We assume that the Old English foot type is the Germanic Foot, a resolved and expanded moraic trochee... The direction of parsing is left to right, and main stress is on the left.' (ms. p.7, sec. 4.1). Middle English: 'The changes sketched above had no effect on the position of main stress, and the stress system in Middle English remained essentially as in Old English. However, the various changes did have the effect of metrically ‘shortening’ words.' (ms. p.9, sec. 4.2); and 'direction of parsing and placement of main stress had not changed before 1530.' (ms. p.10). On French loans in ME: 'words with French stress in Chaucer could in general also be stressed according to the native English pattern, as required by the meter. Hence we find many doublets: (7) citée ~ cítee; comfórt ~ cómfort...' and the French 'stress pattern had no lasting effect on English prosody.' (ms. p.5). Adds to the entry a formal account (Germanic foot, left-to-right parsing, main stress left, secondary stress built left to right), the metrical-shortening claim, the 1530 terminus, and the Chaucer doublets for French loans; all consistent with the entry's stem-syllable rule and its sec. 186 / sec. 215 accent-shift statement.

1402.prule: Germanic root-syllable stress: main accent on the root (Wurzelsilbe), hence always on the first syllable in simplex words; nominal compounds stress the first member, verbal compounds (incl. prefixed verbs ont-, mis-, etc.) stress the verbal part; derivatives keep the accent of the base; nouns with ge-/ver- stress the second element; French loans in -eren/-ieren and -ie keep suffix stress even on Germanic stems.
1402.srule: Secondary stresses (Nebentöne) of several grades: the strongest on compound members that have given up the main accent; in simplex words their position 'läßt sich nicht auf einfache Regeln zurückführen', except that the heavy derivational suffixes (-doem, -heit, -lijk, -scap, -sam, -ijn, -lijn, -kijn, -inghe, -inc, -linc, -ich, -nisse, -âre, -inne, -nede, -ersse, -igghe) always or as a rule carry the strongest secondary stress, independent of the quantity of the main-stressed syllable and of distance from it (their vowels stay full); a rhythmic alternation tendency moves a secondary stress forward (ghèregnéert, ghènatúurt), backward mainly in verse.

dqtr.text: § 15. Just as between the individual syllables of a word, so also between the individual words of a sentence gradations of stress occur. In this a word can subordinate itself to a following or preceding word in such a way that its root syllable can no longer be described as bearing main stress, but only as bearing secondary stress or as unstressed, i.e. that it becomes proclitic or enclitic.

1403.dq: § 15. Wie zwischen den einzelnen silben eines Wortes so finden auch zwischen den einzelnen Wörtern eines satzes abstufungen der betonung statt. Dabei kann sich ein wort dergestalt einem folgenden oder voraufgehenden worte unterordnen, dass seine Wurzelsilbe nicht mehr als haupttonig, sondern nur als nebentonig oder unbetont bezeichnet werden kann, dass es proklitisch oder enklitisch wird.

1403.prule: Simplex word: main stress (hauptton) on the root syllable, which is always the initial syllable; quantity-insensitive. Compounds: nominal compounds stress the root syllable of the first member, verbal compounds (particle/prefix + verb: be-, ge-, en(t)-, er-, ver-, zer-, durch-, über-, under-, umbe-, hinder-, wider-, volle-, misse-) stress the second member; nouns with ge-, ver-, be- also stress the second member.
1403.srule: Secondary stress (nebenton) is present in every word of three or more syllables (§9), but Paul gives no general placement rule for the simplex word: its position does not depend on the quantity of the main-stressed syllable (the older long-root/short-root rule is rejected) and probably varied within the same word with sentence context; only the derivational suffixes -aere, -unge, -nisse, -sal, -inne, -în, -lîn regularly attract it (§10), and in verbal compounds the root syllable of a disyllabic prefix bears it (überwinden), a monosyllabic prefix being unstressed (§13).

1404.dq: At the highest level, the rhyme books are divided into four sections, one for each of the traditional four tonal categories of Middle Chinese: píngshēng 平 聲 ‘level tone’, shǎngshēng 上 聲 ‘rising tone’, qùshēng 去 聲 ‘departing tone’, and rùshēng 入 聲 ‘entering tone’. (Baxter & Sagart 2014:9-10; tone is a property of each syllable/word entry; nothing is said about word- vs phrase-level prominence)
1404.dloc: Baxter & Sagart 2014 p.14, sec. 2.1.2.1; from sec. 2.1.1 pp.9-10.
1404.prule: Four lexical tone categories per (monosyllabic) word/syllable: ping 'level', shang 'rising', qu 'departing', and ru 'entering' (ru = all and only syllables closed by -p, -t, -k), the top-level organising principle of the Qieyun rhyme books (Baxter & Sagart 2014:9-10, 14). dqtr.text: However, since in Huitoto the stress is always on the first or second syllable, it is easier to describe the stress by looking at the first syllables of a word. This is especially important when a word has many syllables.

1409.dq: Sin embargo, como en huitoto el acento siempre está en la primera o segunda sílaba, es más fácil describir el acento al mirar las primeras sílabas de una palabra. Esto es especialmente importante cuando una palabra tiene muchas sílabas.
1409.dloc: Segunda lección, 'El acento', p. 6 (scanned copy, page read + scan; fetched via the Internet Archive copy of the sil.org REAP 16189 URL)
1409.prule: Word accent always falls on the first or second syllable ('el acento siempre está en la primera o segunda sílaba', p. 6); which of the two is not derivable from syllable count and is marked with a tilde where it departs from Spanish defaults (jófo 'casa' vs jitó 'hijo', nahí, benó; nágarui, ácata vs jofómo, jofómona, benómona). The grammar also states morphological conditioning inside the window: in the near future 'El acento siempre se da en la primera sílaba de la palabra' (jiródɨcue 'tomo' ~ jíroitɨcue 'tomaré', macádɨo ~ mácaitɨo, bite ~ bíite, p. 24; negative future jíroñeitɨcue, p. 26); the collective plural 'por lo general' shifts the accent to the first syllable (amena ~ ame, nofɨcɨ ~ nófɨe, p. 34); negative -ñe leaves it unchanged ('El acento no se cambia', p. 16). No weight, vowel-length or tone conditioning is stated.
1409.srule: Not mentioned in Minor, Minor & Levinsohn 1982 ('El acento', p. 6; affixal accent notes pp. 16, 24, 26, 34): the grammar describes one accent per word (first or second syllable) and writes a single accent even on 6-7-syllable words (dúcɨdiaillɨnoɨ, fuénidɨfuiaɨredɨno). The authors' phonology sketch likewise rests on 'un acento-tono alto por cada palabra' (Minor & Minor 1976: 65); no source read describes secondary or rhythmic stress.
1409.quote: El acento. En huitoto las palabras se acentúan lo mismo como en español. Al diferirse la pronunciación el acento se marca. Las palabras de dos o tres sílabas que se acentúan en la sílaba penúltima (palabras graves o llanas) no llevan una tilde. Ejemplos: "jofo" casa, "jofomo" a la casa. Las palabras de dos sílabas que se acentúan en la última sílaba (palabras agudas) siempre llevan una tilde. Ejemplos: "jitó" hijo, "nahí" verdadero, "benó" acá. Las palabras de tres o más sílabas que se acentúan en la sílaba antepenúltima o trasantepenúltima (palabras esdrújulas y sobreesdrújulas) llevan tilde…

Inside it: 'El acento siempre se da en la primera sílaba de la palabra' (near future, p. 24; neg. future p. 26); 'por lo general el acento cambia a la primera sílaba' (collective plural, p. 34)
1409.tone: The 1982 accent section (p.6) says nothing about tone or pitch. Wojtylak 2017 ch.1 fn.2 (in the copy consulted): 'With regards to the lack of tonal distinction, all 'Witoto' dialects are similar to Nonuya but are unlike Ocaina... only Murui and Mɨka have fixed accent position (word-initial). Mɨnɨka and Nɨpode appear to have different patterns of accent placement. This has lead other researchers to hypothesize that it could possibly be indicative of tonal contrasts in Mɨnɨka (Ávila, 2016; Seifart & Fagua Rincón, 2009).' -- i.e. no tone contrast established, a hypothesis only. tn.quote: El acento /´/ es un fonema contrastivo y está acompañado de tono alto: /íθide/ 'hacer daño o mal', /iθíde/ 'cerner'. Cuando el acento de la palabra fonológica cae en la primera vocal de un grupo de vocales, el tono descendente que resulta es un deslizamiento de tono alto a tono bajo [V́.V̀] y puede dar el efecto de un contraste posible de tono. ... Sin embargo, el acento fonémico se ha basado en la ocurrencia consistente de un acento-tono alto por cada palabra, resultando en un análisis menos complicado.
tn.translation: The accent /´/ is a contrastive phoneme and is accompanied by high tone: /íθide/ 'to harm', /iθíde/ 'to sift'. When the accent of the phonological word falls on the first vowel of a vowel group, the resulting falling tone is a glide from high to low tone [V́.V̀] and can give the effect of a possible tone contrast. ... However, the phonemic accent has been based on the consistent occurrence of one accent-high tone per word, resulting in a less complicated analysis.

1410.prule: Word stress (accento tónico) is not fixed: it may fall on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable 'as in Spanish and Portuguese' (oxytone detener, paroxytone cheno, proparoxytone ourégano); with enclitics the accent of the group can fall before the antepenult (ultra-esdrúxulas, fúrã-se-le). Monosyllables are oxytone or atonic. Some words carry a secondary accent (lindamente, on lin-). No weight or positional rule is given; position is a lexical/etymological property (three-syllable right-edge window).

morph.rootq: General statement is purely positional (vol. I §29 pp.205-206): 'O accento tónico ... póde recair na última syllaba, na penúltima ou na ante-penultima, como em hespanhol e português, do que resulta serem as palavras mirandesas: oxytonas ou agudas; ex.: detener; paroxytonas ou graves; ex.: cheno; proparoxytonas ou esdrúxulas; ex.: ourégano. Ha também palavras mirandesas em que, em virtude da énclise (§ 35), o accento recai alem da ante-penultima syllaba, como fúrã-se-le.' But the verb morphology is stated in root terms: §226 p.379 'offerece ó nas flexões rhizotonicas (§ 58), e o nas arhizotonicas: colho, colhes, colhe, colhemos (= culhemos)...'; §227 pp.382-383 '4. Posição do accento tónico…
morph.elicq: No method is stated for the accent section (§§28-35), which cites isolated words (detener, cheno, ourégano) and one enclitic group (fúrã-se-le). The evidential basis of the whole grammar is the author's own auditory fieldwork: §253 note 2, p.407: 'Todas as formas que cito a cima, como todas as que, sem alguma indicação especial, cito nesta obra, as ouvi eu mesmo dizer.'; Advertência preambular p.169: 'foi meu único intuito estudar os phenomenos glotticos que se relacionam com os textos publicados no Volume II d'esta obra' (folk tales, songs and conversation transcribed 'da boca do povo', e.g. §252 p.405 'num conto popular que trasladei da boca do povo'). No instrumental or frame-sentence…
morph.stmt: Mirandese as described by Leite de Vasconcellos is a suffixing language of the Ibero-Romance type: all nominal and verbal inflection is by endings after the root/theme ('As desinências do pres. do indic. vêem-se no seguinte quadro: -o, -a-s, -a-, -a-mos, -a-is, -ã', §216; plural 'a terminação -s... -es', §163), word formation is treated under a long 'Suffixação' list (§298: -ico, -ito, -inho, -uco, -õu/-ona, -eiro, -és, -al, -ada, -ança, -iar, -ecer, -mente...) against a short 'Prefixação' (§299: des-, ã-/an-/am- < in-, prothetic a-), with the author remarking that 'os processos adoptados pelo mirandês para a formação de palavras novas não differem essencialmente dos que o português…

1412.prule: No stress system is described for any Miyako variety. Word-level prosody is tonal and dialect-dependent: Irabu is 'accentless' (no lexical prosody) but has a predictable foot-based tonal rhythm — morae are parsed into bi-/trimoraic feet, feet into groups of up to three, and /H/ is assigned to the left-most foot of each foot group (H vs toneless alternation); Ikema has the same non-distinctive trochaic tonal rhythm plus a two-way lexical word-tone contrast (type α falling / type β rising-level) realised at the right edge of the lexical word; Ōgami has no fixed lexical pitch pattern at all.

1414.dq: Greek is a bounded system; the scope of primary stress is limited to the last three syllables of the word.
1414.prule: Lexical accent system: primary stress falls on any of the last three syllables (three-syllable window), position determined by inherent accentual marking of roots/suffixes (accented, pre-accenting, unaccentable) and their competition; weight plays no role.
1414.srule: Optional rhythmic secondary stress only: when two or more syllables precede the primary stress, alternate syllables to its left may carry secondary stress in trochaic feet, e.g. (pire)(ás), (trape)(záki) (Revithiadou 1999, after Malikouti-Drachman & Drachman 1981); acoustic and perceptual studies find these syllables indistinguishable from unstressed ones, and the phonetic literature treats Greek words as carrying a single stress (Arvaniti 2007).
1414.quote: Greek syllable structure lacks distinctions of phonological weight; all syllables are of equal phonological weight (Joseph and Philippaki 1987). evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: The article argues, within Distributed Morphology, that Greek derivational affixes are categorizers rather than roots, using their stress behaviour as the key evidence: Greek has one lexical stress per word within the final three syllables, and the derivational affix (most of which are themselves stressed; -imos and -ma impose antepenultimate stress) fixes the word's stress regardless of the root, whereas in root-plus-inflection combinations the root wins. 1415.prule: Stress falls on the final syllable before a pause (phrase-/utterance-final, pre-pausal); the stressed syllable requires a full vowel (epenthetic vowel -> full counterpart). Words in isolation (citation form) therefore surface with final-syllable stress, but the rule is stated over the pre-pausal phrase, not the word. No weight condition; no word-level stress rule given. Language also has a two-tone (H/L underlying; H, M, L phonetic) lexical and grammatical tone system with low lexical load.
1415.quote: The third basic factor is that the final syllable before a pause is stressed in pronunciation. The stressed syllable necessitates a full vowel, meaning that any epenthetic vowel in that syllable will be changed to its full counterpart. 1417.dq: With reference to word level stress, it is not always to be clearly established, because in general the Mori speak very rapidly, and use strong rhetorical accents, so that the words which do not attract such a discourse-accent receive only minor stress.
1417.dloc: Section 17 'STRESS' (orig. pp. 14-16; e-book pp. 10-11), incl. footnotes 12-13
1417.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (enclitics count: stress shifts rightward when an enclitic is added); monosyllables are clitics and unstressed; long vowels count as two syllables; secondary stress on the initial syllable of four-syllable words (or on the original stress site of the stem in affixed words/compounds); loans with original final stress lengthen the final vowel so stress is still penultimate.
1417.srule: Esser (sec. 17): in four-syllable words secondary stress generally on the initial syllable; in compounds and in words with a polysyllabic prefix or suffix the stem keeps a secondary stress where its own penultimate stress originally fell (mompókokodéi, domédudúngkuakóno), non-final compound members being reduced to secondary; loan mantaríi has secondary on ma. Barsel 1994 (sec. 2.3.2) restates this from her own data as a morpheme-based rule: secondary stress on the penultimate syllable of every bi- or trisyllabic morpheme or morpheme cluster to the left of the primary stress (me,'ala,'ala'kiko;mepetu,lungi 'aku;paralu'uno).
1417.quote: 17. STRESS. As a rule, a stem in Mori (a fortiori a word) consists of two or more syllables. ... one-syllable words are in Mori, just as in Pamona, always proclitics or enclitics. Stress in Mori is placed on the penultimate syllable, so that the language is missing an important tool for keeping oneself aware of the derivation of words formed with suffixes. For stress placement the same applies of enclitics, so that one says for example ambáu 'carabao', …

1418.dq: With reference to word level stress, it is not always to be clearly established, because in general the Mori speak very rapidly, and use strong rhetorical accents, so that the words which do not attract such a discourse-accent receive only minor stress.
1418.dloc: Esser/Mead 2011, Chapter 1 section 17 'Stress' (orig. pp. 14-16; e-book ch.1 pp. 9-10, pp. 33-34); scope of the name 'Mori' in section 1 (orig. p. 3); Mead 1999 Appendix 3 p.101 item (g). Mead 1998 PhD sec. 3.1.2 'Syllable patterns and stress', p. 97: 'All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages also exhibit penultimate stress.'
1418.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (enclitics included in the count: ambáu -> ambaúmo); monosyllables are clitics and unstressed; long vowels count as two syllables (opáa).
1418.srule: Secondary stress on the initial syllable of four-syllable words (e.g. mantarii: ri primary, ma secondary); in compounds and in words with a prefix or suffix of more than one syllable the stem keeps a secondary stress where its own stress originally fell (hóri akúmo, domédudúngkuakóno, mompókokodéi), primary remaining on the word penult; non-final compound members are demoted to secondary. Esser notes secondary stress is often hard to establish under rhetorical accent (fn. 3 p. 16). Placement in simple words of 5+ syllables not stated.
